extracted.intended_audience: federal judges and patent litigators preparing or using jury instructions in patent trials (AIPLA Model Patent Jury Instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent litigation covering invalidity defenses (prior invention, prior patents, earlier-filed applications), obviousness (Graham factors), enablement, written-description, and damages. Designed to be adapted and given to juries in federal patent trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Invention (Pre-AIA Only)
rubrics_metrics.description: That patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was invented by [third party] before [the patentee] invented his invention, [and that other person did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The Defendant] must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before [the patentee] invented his invention, [third party] reduced to practice a [[product] [method]] that included all of the features of claim ___, or (2) [third party] was first to conceive the invention and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. In addition, [third party]'s [[product] [method]] must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized that it would work for its intended purpose. Practice Note: this defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is asserted, the jury should be instructed that a prior invention does not anticipate if the prior inventor actively concealed the invention or unreasonably delayed public disclosure. Generally there is no abandonment/suppression/concealment if the invention was made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially; delay is not necessarily concealment if reasonable efforts to bring the invention to market occurred. Burden: clear and convincing evidence. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (Pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country [by [third party] before [§102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]] [before [§102(b) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual issue for the jury about the date of invention of the patent claims in suit or the priority date, the jury should be instructed on how to determine that date; otherwise the Court should instruct the jury as to the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: if there is a factual issue as to whether disclosure in a patent resulted from the inventor/joint inventor or from someone who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor (or whether it had been publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor or someone who obtained it from the inventor), then the jury should be instructed about exceptions under §102(b)(1), as needed. The instruction should reference the effective filing date of the claimed invention. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102(a)(1), 102(b)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (Pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was described in [[U.S.] [international PCT]] [[published patent application] [patent]] filed by another person before that invention was invented by [the patentee].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used where the filing date of an application is the relevant date. If there is a factual issue as to the date of invention of the claims in suit, the jury should be instructed on how to determine that date; otherwise the Court should instruct as to the date of invention. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102(e)(1) and (2) (pre-AIA) and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [That] patent claim[s] [[is] [are]] invalid if the invention defined by [[that] [those]] claim[s] was described in a (1) published U.S. patent application, (2) issued U.S. patent, or (3) published international PCT patent application that designates the U.S., filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: If there is a factual issue as to whether disclosure in a patent application was subject matter obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor, publicly disclosed by the inventor or another who obtained it from the inventor, or was owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person, then the jury should be instructed on exceptions under §§102(b)(2) and (c), as needed. The instruction should include the effective filing date of the claimed invention and the effective filing date of the published patent application (per 35 U.S.C. §102(d)). (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102(a)(2), (b)(2), (c), & (d) (AIA); 35 U.S.C. §374.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—General (Graham Framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art of the claimed invention as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, which allows consideration of only one item of prior art, obviousness may be shown by considering one or more items of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must avoid hindsight and not use the patent as a roadmap for selecting/combining prior art. The following four factors (Graham factors) must be evaluated separately for each claim: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date; (4) additional considerations (secondary considerations). [The Defendant] bears the burden of proving obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; KSR v. Teleflex; Graham v. John Deere; Apple v. Samsung.)

rubrics_metrics.name: First Graham Factor: Scope and Content of the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding obviousness, the prior art includes the items received into evidence during the trial (and any stipulated prior art). A prior art reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem or need addressed by the patent or has obvious uses beyond its main purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether [the Defendant] has proven by clear and convincing evidence that a specific reference is prior art. Practice Note: If the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger’s burden may be easier to sustain; jury may be instructed to evaluate whether evidence is materially new compared to what the PTO considered. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i and other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Graham Factor: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether there are any relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the view of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date, determining the impact of such differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require precise prior-art teaching directed to the claimed subject matter; consider inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would have used. If a claimed combination yielded predictable results or there was a reason to combine prior art, that supports obviousness; unexpected results or teachings away support nonobviousness. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine prior art and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. If a reference teaches away, it discourages combining. Inherency: inherency may supply a missing claim element only if the element is the natural result of the explicit disclosure (not by probabilities/possibilities); tailor inherency instruction to evidence and only give if properly raised and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Graham Factor: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, you must determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the Cutoff Date; the person of ordinary skill is presumed to know all prior art determined reasonably relevant and is a person of ordinary creativity who can use common sense to solve problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties agree on the skill level, include their agreed statement. If not, consider evidence including: (1) level of education and experience of persons working in the field as of the Cutoff Date (including the inventor(s)); (2) types of problems encountered and prior art solutions; (3) sophistication of the technology and rapidity of innovations as of the Cutoff Date. Assess this factor before reaching an obviousness conclusion. (Cites: KSR; Graham.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Graham Factor: Secondary Considerations (Other Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider secondary factors that may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious, recognizing no single factor is dispositive and the invention should be considered as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (1) commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention rather than advertising or other non-claimed features; (2) long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention; (3) others tried but failed; (4) others copied the invention; (5) unexpectedly superior results; (6) praise or expressed surprise; (7) acceptance of licenses due to the merits. These factors are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the patentee bears the burden of showing a sufficient nexus. Court must consider admissibility of such evidence and only instruct the jury when supported by the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable or teach persons of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; this is the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The Defendant] bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy enablement. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill, so a patent need not expressly state information persons of ordinary skill would know. Factors to consider in determining whether undue experimentation would be required include: (1) quantity of experimentation necessary and whether it involves only known or commonly used techniques; (2) amount of direction or guidance disclosed in the patent; (3) presence or absence of working examples in the patent; (4) nature of the invention; (5) state of the prior art; (6) relative skill of those in the art; (7) predictability of the art; and (8) breadth of the claims. Enablement is a question of law for the Court; jury only on subsidiary fact issues if specific factual disputes bearing on enablement are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must contain a written description of the [[product] [method]] claimed in the patent; the written-description requirement helps ensure that the patent applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The Defendant] bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the written-description requirement. To satisfy written description, the specification must describe each and every limitation of a patent claim with clear, concise, and exact terms; the claim must be viewed as a whole. The requirement is satisfied if persons of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the subject matter finally claimed as of the effective filing date, even if claims were changed later. Exact words need not be used and specific examples are not required, but enough must be included to convince those skilled in the art that the inventor possessed the full scope of the invention. Factors to consider include: (1) nature and scope of the patent claims; (2) complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; (3) existing knowledge in the field; (4) scope and content of the prior art. Sufficiency is decided claim-by-claim. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §112 and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—General Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that the accused [[device] [method]] infringes any asserted claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded the Plaintiff for the infringement. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement and put the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in had the infringement not occurred. Damages cannot be punitive or include interest; reasonable royalty is the minimum amount recoverable. Do not consider damages if all asserted claims are invalid or not infringed. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §284 and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin / Notice and Marking
rubrics_metrics.description: The start date for damages is either the date stipulated by the parties or, if disputed, the date the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two ways to give notice: (1) public notice by marking substantially all products practicing the invention with the patent number (or 'Patent'/'Pat' plus a freely accessible Internet address linking product to patent number); licensees who use the invention must also mark substantially all their products; marking is effective even if the Defendant did not see it. (2) Direct notice to the Defendant with a specific claim that the product infringed; notice starts on the date Defendant received it. If Plaintiff failed to provide effective marking or direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can only recover damages for infringement after filing suit, except that if no patented products were made/sold (e.g., only method claims asserted), Plaintiff may recover damages up to six years before filing suit. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§286, 287(a) and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Kinds of Recoverable Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary kinds of damages are available for patent infringement: lost profits and a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits: additional profits the patentee would have made 'but for' the defendant's infringement; may include related or collateral product profits or price effects under certain circumstances. Reasonable royalty: the amount a willing licensee would have paid a willing licensor just before infringement began; a reasonable royalty is the minimum recoverable award. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §284 and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—'But For' Test
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] is seeking lost-profits damages. To prove lost profits, [the Plaintiff] must show that, but for [the Defendant]'s infringement, [the Plaintiff] would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales of the allegedly infringing products made by [the Defendant].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove lost profits by a preponderance of the evidence. The jury must determine what purchasers of the accused product would have done if infringement had not occurred. The relevant profits are those lost by the Plaintiff, not profits made by the Defendant on infringing sales.
